title: Soundscape and natural landscape as a design construct for improving psycho-physiological health in cities: a semi-systematic literature review
authors: Timothy Onosahwo Iyendo, David Welch & Patrick Chukwuemeke Uwajeh (2024)
review_question: To explore the effects of natural landscape and positive soundscape, with a specific emphasis on their influence on physical and mental health within urban environments, addressing health and planning perspectives.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies published in English between January 2000 and 2022, dealing with positive soundscape and natural landscape pertaining to physiological, psychological, or physio-psychological health improvements. Excluded: papers not explicitly addressing physio-psychological health effects or planning/design aspects, book reviews, monographs, duplicates, encyclopaedia articles, non-English publications, editorials, and studies investigating music and hard-scapes.

synthesis_conclusions: Natural landscape and soundscape profoundly impact psychological and physiological health.

Water features, bird calls, and vegetation reduce noise, improve perceived landscape/soundscape quality, enhance comfort, enjoyment, biodiversity, and improve emotional, recreational, social, cultural, cognitive, behavioral, physical, and physiological health.

Well-designed multisensory built environments integrating natural vegetation and natural sound sources (pleasant water, soothing bird song) can create safe, healthy urban environments and enhance residents' psychophysiological health.
Exposure to natural soundscapes and landscape environments through interactive display technologies or audio-visual interactions improves psychophysiological responses.

Technological tools are useful for participatory soundscape/landscape planning, predicting multisensory environment influence, improving soundscape/landscape quality, solving social problems, improving quality of life, relieving stress, and stimulating brain regions for physiological/psychological relaxation.
evidence_gaps: Need for larger samples and focus on diverse demographics (ethnicities, ages, genders, people with disabilities, socio-economics) to understand sensescapes.
Further research is needed to comprehend unique requirements and preferences of blind people in natural settings.
Research should move beyond single sensory modalities to include other sensory modalities (olfaction, temperature, tactile) and other aspects of urban life for a holistic urban context.
Lack of knowledge on how landscapes and soundscapes influence health, especially how positive sensescapes influence health-promoting thoughts and behaviors.

Need to improve understanding of causal connections between natural surroundings and human health using robust study designs and interdisciplinary investigations (environmental psychology, urban planning, landscape architecture, ecology, health sciences, neuroscience).
More multidimensional investigations are required to gain a deeper understanding of psychophysiological effects.
risk_of_bias_assessment: The two reviewers independently assessed the quality of the studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted if necessary.
heterogeneity_sources: Heterogeneity of study designs, interventions, and outcomes measured
limitations: Limited findings on the impact of pleasant soundscape and natural landscape on physiological measures.
Limited research in these areas, requiring more data to clarify and extend findings.
Small sample sizes and exploratory nature of some pilot studies limit generalizability, requiring larger samples for validation.
